title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, and which languages you speak — while fitting in the negative *nu* and the first verb group: the one with the *-esc* insert.
bekal: ask and say where someone is from with *de unde* and *din*, and where they live with *unde* and *în*
make any sentence negative with the single word *nu* — no "do/does" needed
conjugate *a vorbi* and *a locui*, and give nationalities in the masculine and feminine

dialogs.title: Dialogue — În pauza de prânz
dialogs.intro: Lunch break at the office. Ioana invites her friend Maria to eat with them and introduces her to Budi.

lines.speaker: Ioana:
lines.text: Budi, ea este Maria, prietena mea.
lines.id: Budi, this is Maria, my friend.
lines.literal: Budi, she she-is Maria, friend-f-the my-f.

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.id: Hi, Budi! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Din Indonezia! Și unde locuiești acum?
lines.id: From Indonesia! And where do you live now?
lines.literal: from-in Indonesia! and where you-live now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Acum locuiesc în București, cu Andrei. El este din Cluj.
lines.id: Now I live in București, with Andrei. He's from Cluj.
lines.literal: now I-live in București, with Andrei. he he-is from-in Cluj.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Puțin. Încă nu vorbesc bine. Scuze!
lines.id: A little. I don't speak well yet. Sorry!
lines.literal: little. still not I-speak well. excuses!

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Nu-i nimic. Vorbești foarte bine! Ce limbi vorbești?
lines.id: It's nothing. You speak very well! Which languages do you speak?
lines.literal: not-it-is nothing. you-speak very well! what languages you-speak?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vorbesc indoneziană, engleză și puțin română. Tu ești româncă?
lines.id: I speak Indonesian, English, and a little Romanian. Are you Romanian?
lines.literal: I-speak Indonesian-f, English-f and little Romanian-f. you you-are Romanian-f?

lines.speaker: Maria:
lines.text: Da, sunt româncă, dar nu sunt din București. Sunt din Sibiu.
lines.id: Yes, I'm Romanian, but I'm not from București. I'm from Sibiu.
lines.literal: yes, I-am Romanian-f, but not I-am from-in București. I-am from-in Sibiu.

lines.speaker: Ioana:
lines.text: Maria vorbește și germană. La birou vorbim engleză, dar în pauză vorbim românește.
lines.id: Maria speaks German too. At the office we speak English, but on our break we speak Romanian.
lines.literal: Maria she-speaks also German-f. at office we-speak English-f, but in break we-speak Romanian-way.

notes: **De unde ești? — ask with *de*, answer with *din*.** *Unde* = where, *de unde* = from where. The answer uses *din*, a merger of *de* + *în*: "from in". To someone you address formally: *De unde sunteți?* Notice that the verb is still *a fi* — just like English, Romanians "are from" a place.
**Încă nu = not yet.** *Încă* (still) + *nu* (not). The order is fixed and *nu* always sits right in front of its verb: *Încă nu vorbesc bine*, *Încă nu sunt gata*.

**Nu-i nimic literally means "it isn't nothing".** *Nu-i* is a shortened *nu este*, and *nimic* means "nothing". Two negatives at once — and in Romanian that's required, not a mistake. It's the standard reply when someone apologizes.

**Românește is not the name of the language but a manner.** *Vorbesc românește* literally means "I speak in the Romanian way". The language itself is *româna* or *limba română*. Both are equally common: *Vorbești românește?* = *Vorbești română?*

**Și means both "and" and "also".** Between two things it's "and": *engleză și română*. In front of one word it's "also, too": *Maria vorbește și germană* = "Maria speaks German **too**". You already used it in unit 1 without noticing: *Și eu* — "me too".

grammars.title: Nu — one negative for everything
body: English needs a helper to say no: *I **don't** speak*, *she **isn't***. Romanian doesn't bother: just put **nu** right in front of the verb, whatever you are negating.
after: ***Nu* also means "no" as an answer**, so it often appears twice in a row with different jobs: *Nu, nu sunt din București* — the first answers, the second negates. At the end of a sentence, *nu?* becomes "right?": *Ești student, nu?*

**Double negatives are required.** Words like *nimic* (nothing), *nimeni* (nobody), and *niciodată* (never) always come with *nu*: *Nu înțeleg nimic* = "I don't understand anything" (literally "I don't understand nothing"). Leaving out the *nu* is what's wrong.

**In conversation, *nu* likes to merge with the next word**: *nu este → nu-i*, and *nu am → n-am* ("I don't have" — the verb *a avea* comes in unit 3). You don't have to use these, but you do have to recognize them, because that's how people talk.

grammars.title: A vorbi and a locui — verbs with the -esc insert
body: A Romanian infinitive is always preceded by the little word *a*, just like English "to": *a vorbi* (to speak), *a locui* (to live). Most verbs ending in *-i* slip **-esc-** in between the stem and the ending — but only in four of the six forms.
after: **The insert disappears in *noi* and *voi*.** In those two forms the stress moves to the ending (vohr-BEEM, vohr-BEETS'), and *-esc-* isn't needed any more. In the other four forms the stress always falls on the insert. The *sc* softens to *șt* before *i* and *e*: *-esc, -ești, -ește*.
**The *eu* and *ei/ele* forms are twins**, just like *sunt* in unit 1: *vorbesc* = "I speak" and "they speak". Only when context isn't clear does the pronoun come out: *Ei vorbesc germană*.

**This pattern unlocks dozens of verbs at once**: *a citi* (citesc — to read), *a dori* (doresc — to wish), *a plăti* (plătesc — to pay), *a găti* (gătesc — to cook), and the one you've used since day one: *a mulțumi* → *mulțumesc*, *mulțumim*. Not every *-i* verb follows this pattern (unit 8), so this course's vocabulary lists always give the *eu* form in brackets.

blocks.text: **Lowercase.** Only country names are capitalized; nationalities and languages are written in lowercase — unlike English: *Sunt indonezian. Vorbesc engleză.* And as with jobs in unit 1, a nationality after *a fi* takes no article.

**The feminine form has three possible endings, and you have to learn them word by word**: *-că* (*româncă, indoneziancă, italiancă*), *-oaică* (*englezoaică, franțuzoaică, chinezoaică*), or just *-ă* (*germană, olandeză, japoneză*). Learn the one for your own nationality first — Budi's are *indonezian* [een-doh-neh-zee-AHN] and *indoneziancă* [een-doh-neh-zee-AHN-kuh].

**Language name = the feminine form of the adjective**, because it follows the word *limbă* (language), which is feminine: *limba română*, *limba engleză*. Some languages also have a "manner" form ending in *-ește*: *românește, englezește, franțuzește, nemțește* (the German way), *ungurește*. This form is used only with verbs like *a vorbi* and never changes. Indonesian has no common *-ește* form, so Budi says *vorbesc indoneziană*.

blocks.title: A Latin island in Eastern Europe
items: Romanian is a sister of Italian, French, Spanish, and Portuguese — all descendants of Latin. The name *România* itself comes from the word *roman*. Its neighbors, though, speak Slavic languages and Hungarian, so Romania is often called a Latin island in Eastern Europe. The same language is also spoken in the Republic of Moldova.

Transylvania — including Cluj, Andrei's hometown — is home to many Hungarian speakers. Sibiu, Maria's hometown, was built by German settlers (the *sași*, Saxons) in the Middle Ages and has a German name: Hermannstadt. That's why Maria speaks German.
Good news for you: much of that Latin vocabulary already looks familiar from English — *familie, problemă, muzică, doctor, universitate, informație*.

sections.title: Din versus în — from where and where

blocks.text: Two questions, two prepositions, and they pair up neatly. The ones beginners mix up most are *din* and *de*, so look closely at the examples column.

head: Word
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Sunt din Indonezia. El este din Cluj.*
at; to (a point: office, station, event)
*Sunt la birou. Vorbim engleză la birou.*

blocks.text: The formula: **unde → în**, **de unde → din**. Countries and cities always use this pair: *în Indonezia — din Indonezia*, *în Sibiu — din Sibiu*. The preposition *la* is used for places seen as a point or an activity, not a space you're inside: *la birou* (at the office), *la universitate* (at university). The difference between *în* and *la* is sorted out in unit 6; for now, learn the examples.

head: Language lifesavers
English
rows: I understand, but I can't speak.
What language do you speak at home?

blocks.text: Romanians almost always greet your attempts at Romanian with praise — *Vorbești foarte bine!* — even if you only know three sentences. Just accept it with *Mulțumesc!* and carry on in Romanian. Switching to English at that moment is the fastest way to stop learning.
